source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: With an oracle label deciding when to stop, self-correction helps. Without the label (intrinsic), accuracy falls on nearly every benchmark.
numbers: Oracle, GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9->84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8->89.7, HotpotQA 26.0->29.0. Oracle, GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5->97.5, CSQA 82.0->85.5, HotpotQA 49->59. Intrinsic, GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9->75.1->74.7 (rounds 1,2), CSQA 75.8->38.1->41.8, HotpotQA 26->25->25. Intrinsic, GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5->91.5->89.0, CSQA 82.0->79.5->80.0, HotpotQA 49->49->43.
limits: Two rounds only. HotpotQA sample is 100 items. Table layout was garbled by PDF extraction; numbers read as best matched to the text.
agent_relevance: A frame switch triggered by the model's own doubt hurts. Switch only on an external failure signal (G1, G2). Matches the Kuhn view that anomalies must be real, not felt.

source: Huang et al. (2024) why self-correction fails
finding: After self-correction the model more often turns a right answer into a wrong one than the reverse, because it cannot judge the correctness of its own reasoning.
numbers: GPT-3.5 keeps its initial GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time after two rounds. CommonSenseQA answers change much more often. GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo retain their first answer more often than GPT-3.5 or Llama-2.
limits: Prompts follow the source papers and differ across tasks.
agent_relevance: False-switch cost is real. Set the anomaly bar high enough that correct answers are not overturned.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Survey of self-correction work to May 2024. No prior work shows successful self-correction using feedback from a prompted LLM on general tasks. It works with reliable external feedback and after large-scale fine-tuning. The bottleneck is feedback generation.
numbers: Qualitative: three conclusions (no success with prompted-LLM feedback outside tasks suited to it; external feedback works; large-scale fine-tuning works). No pooled effect size.
quote: no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Abstract and introduction read closely; later sections only skimmed. Many positive papers use oracle stopping or weak baselines.
agent_relevance: Supports counting verifier failures in code rather than asking the model. A 'several independent failures' trigger must count external failures.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) checklist for fair self-correction tests
finding: The survey gives a checklist: state the research question, use a realistic feedback source, use a fair baseline. Tasks that split into verifiable parts suit self-correction.
numbers: Checklist in section 8; no numbers.
limits: Section 8 not read in full.
agent_relevance: Use the checklist to grade our S6 test: no oracle stopping, equal-compute baseline.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models are poor at finding the first wrong step but good at fixing it once told where it is. Locating the anomaly is the bottleneck, not the repair.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 5 tasks. GPT-4 best, 52.87% overall mistake-location accuracy with direct step prompting. Backtracking with true location: change in accuracy on originally incorrect traces +23.53, +43.92, +36.86, +18.04, +18.06 points; on originally correct traces -11.11, -6.67, -11.43, 0.00, -6.82. Random location: +11.76, +20.39, +21.57, +10.59, +5.16 on incorrect traces; -15.56, -6.67, -13.33, -8.89, -15.91 on correct traces.
limits: PaLM 2 Unicorn used for correction. Task-to-column mapping in the table was garbled by extraction.
agent_relevance: Frame switches need a located failure. Locate the failing step by code (test, checker), not by asking the model.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) mistake finding vs trained classifier
finding: Prompted models barely beat a trivial baseline for judging whether a trace is right. A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data finds mistakes better than prompting a large model.
numbers: Weighted F1 for predicting every trace incorrect is 78. GPT-4 per-task location accuracy: tracking shuffled objects 62.29, logical deduction 40.67.
limits: Five tasks; traces generated by PaLM 2.
agent_relevance: A small trained anomaly detector may beat asking the main model. Candidate part of an S6 trigger.

source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong
finding: On graph colouring GPT-4 is poor at solving and no better at verifying. Self-critique does not beat baseline. With a sound external verifier about 40% are solved, but the content of the feedback hardly matters.
numbers: 100 instances. Of 100 optimal colourings the LLM verifier accepted only 2. Of 500 colourings (118 correct) it called 30 correct and was right 5 times. It stopped only 4 of 100 runs, none correct. Binary vs single-error vs full-error feedback: differences insignificant.
limits: One task family, GPT-4 only, 2023.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation for 'reframe after failures': the gain may be resampling. Test S6 against equal-compute best-of-N (G4).

source: Stechly et al. (2023) resampling control
finding: Counting any-time-correct answers, LLM self-critique reaches about 40%, the same as sound-verifier runs. Number of tries matters more than feedback. Separate non-interacting samples at higher temperature rival the loops.
numbers: 100 instances; all four back-prompt types roughly similar at about 40% when any correct colouring counts.
limits: Final resampling table not read in full.
agent_relevance: Every S6 test needs an equal-budget resampling arm.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: After a failed trial the agent writes a short lesson and tries again. An anomaly-driven revision loop with an external success signal.
numbers: ALFWorld, 134 tasks: ReAct+Reflexion solved 130 of 134 in 12 trials. ReAct-only stopped improving between trials 6 and 7, hallucination rate stuck near 22%. Paper reports +22% absolute ALFWorld, +20% HotpotQA, +11% HumanEval (91% pass@1).
limits: Stop signal is a heuristic or ground truth. Huang et al. say ground-truth stopping inflates such gains.
agent_relevance: A working form of switching after failures: external trigger, stored diagnosis, retry. Copy the memory step, not a self-judged trigger.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models switch lines of thought too often and abandon promising lines. Wrong answers contain far more switches.
numbers: Incorrect responses use 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones (QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1; MATH500, GPQA Diamond, AIME2024).
limits: Two open o1-like models; AIME2024 has only 30 problems (plus 60 from 2022-23).
agent_relevance: The opposite failure to anchoring: premature revolution. Kuhn's crisis needs sustained, converging anomaly, so set a minimum dwell time before S6 fires.

source: Wang et al. (2025) thought-switching penalty (TIP) results
finding: Penalising switch tokens in decoding raises accuracy, with a dose-response. Too long a strong penalty hurts.
numbers: Pass@1 AIME2024: QwQ 38.3->44.1, R1-Distill-32B 61.4->64.1, DeepSeek-R1 73.8->74.8. QwQ pass@4 53.7->61.6, pass@16 62.7->74.0. QwQ GPQA 57.6->59.1; MATH500-Hard 83.1->83.7. Switch tokens per response QwQ AIME 16.1->13.9; R1 13.8->5.7. Chosen strength 3, duration 600; at strength 20 durations beyond 300 reduce accuracy.
limits: Tuned on 60 development problems. Decoding penalty, not a prompt rule. Gains on easy sets are tiny.
agent_relevance: Brackets the dwell floor: hundreds of tokens in a frame before switching. Tune per model.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling
finding: Appending 'Wait' when the model tries to stop forces a recheck and sometimes a fix. Longer thinking scales accuracy up to a limit.
numbers: s1-32B: AIME24 50.0 without budget forcing, 56.7 with; MATH500 92.6->93.0; GPQA Diamond 56.6->59.6.
limits: One base model, 1K training examples, AIME24 is 30 problems (one problem is 3.3 points).
agent_relevance: A forced second look helps a little but is a schedule, not a signal (G1). Use it as a baseline arm against a signal-triggered S6.

source: Chu & Evans (2021) Slowed canonical progress in large fields of science, PNAS 118(41)
finding: As a field grows, citations concentrate on already-famous papers and new ideas struggle to enter the canon. This is Kuhn's normal-science lock-in measured at scale.
numbers: Web of Science 1960-2014: 90,637,277 papers, 241 subjects. Spearman correlation of top-50 lists in adjacent years 0.25 at 1,000 papers/yr vs 0.74 at 100,000. Share of papers with disruption D>0: 49% at 1,000, 27% at 10,000, 13% at 100,000. Top-5% disruptive share 8.8% -> 3.6% -> 0.6%. Median wait to reach the top 0.1%: about 9 years at 1,000 papers vs under 1 year at 100,000.
quote: new paradigms arise to structure inquiry
limits: Correlational; other causes not ruled out. Stable top lists do not prove stagnation. Mechanisms (overload, idea competition) are theory.
agent_relevance: More samples of one frame can crowd out a rival. Keep a rival-frame slot that is not outvoted by volume (G4).

source: Chu & Evans (2021) robustness and concentration numbers
finding: Field size acts beyond time and field age. Veteran scholars also cite canon more as fields grow.
numbers: Gini of citation shares about 0.5 in the largest fields. Top 1% of papers hold 8.6% of citations at 10,000 papers/yr, 11.9% at 50,000, 16.7% at 100,000. Papers just outside the top 1% lose about 17% of citations per year; the most cited show no decline at 100,000 papers/yr.
limits: Supplementary tables S1-S3 not opened. Only fields and large subfields.
agent_relevance: Lock-in is partly crowding, not only individual stubbornness; for a multi-sample agent, many correlated samples crowd out the rival.

source: Singh et al. (2022) Quantifying the rise and fall of scientific fields, PLoS ONE 17(6)
finding: Fields follow one rise-and-fall curve. Early-stage fields have more cross-field authors, smaller teams and higher disruption. The paper cites Kuhn (1962) for common stages.
numbers: 1,456,403 arXiv articles to 2018, 175 fields; 72 kept; 66 of 72 (91.6%) fit a Gumbel curve (KS test). Early stage: 2.36 fields per article vs 2.05 late; about 2 authors vs 4.5; career fields 16.9 vs 7.9. Disruption highest at creation.
limits: Descriptive. Only 72 of 175 fields kept. arXiv citations sparse. Gumbel not compared with other shapes; stage cut-offs look arbitrary.
agent_relevance: New frames come from far-apart combinations. For S6 draw the new frame from a distant domain, not a local variant.

source: Klein et al. (2023) The plausibility transition model for sensemaking, Front. Psychol.
finding: Describes when a story is dropped: gaps cannot be filled, strain builds, a tilt occurs, and a search for another story starts. Anomalies grow if the first diagnosis is wrong.
numbers: Literature review: 1,042 articles, 18 strongly relevant, 4 added, 22 analysed. Case set: 73 cases (convenience), 23 analysed by one reviewer. No percentages.
limits: Exploratory and untested; one coder; no Kuhn citation. Its predictions are not yet tested.
agent_relevance: Design hint for S6: keep a count of unfilled gaps and fire when it crosses a threshold, not on one anomaly.

source: Luhmann & Ahn (2011) Expectations and interpretations during causal learning, JEP:LMC
finding: People reinterpret conflicting observations in light of earlier expectations. Extra conflicting trials plus an alternative cause pushed judgments toward the first belief, opposite to Rescorla-Wagner and delta-p predictions.
limits: Undergraduates at two universities, small cells. One reported F(1,31) with 16 participants is inconsistent. Correlational regressions link interpretation and judgment.
agent_relevance: Order and load decide whether early frames dominate: under load the latest data wins. Log early anomalies explicitly so they are not lost in long context.

source: Ecker lab (2025) Did he or didn't he? Mixed evidence for continued influence of retracted misinformation, PLoS ONE
finding: Retracted false information showed a continued influence in only one of three experiments. A mixed and partly failed replication.
numbers: Exp 1 N=301, Exp 2 N=300, Exp 3 N=301 (Prolific). Retraction vs neutral: Exp 2 small effect (likability beta -0.31, p=.003, f2=.04; inference beta 0.49, p<.001, f2=.08). Exp 1 and 3 none (p .161/.084; .516/.832). Meta-analysis of the three: likability -0.13, p=.253; inference 0.25, p=.073. With four earlier experiments added: -0.07 (p=.263), -0.03 (p=.909). Unretracted misinformation had a large effect (f2 up to about 2.4).
limits: Person-impression materials only; US online workers; power set for f2=.04. Earlier work found effects for political or mental-health targets.
agent_relevance: Belief perseverance is real but small and material-dependent. Do not over-build an anchoring guard on it. Kuhn lock-in has better support in citation data than in lab belief updating.

source: Medical Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus study (2025) Limitations of LLMs in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning (mARC-QA), Sci Rep
finding: Questions built to trigger a familiar heuristic with decisive counterevidence (Einstellung style) make LLMs fail where physicians do not.
numbers: 100 items; five physicians averaged 66% (SE 5.3). Best models: DeepSeek-R1 52%, DeepSeek-V3 50%, Gemini 1.5-pro 50%, o1 48%. Several models under 20%; Medalpaca and Meditron near 0%. About 53% of items offer a seek-more-data option. Models overconfident, small ones more.
limits: Only 100 authors' items, five human raters, no construct validation of Einstellung, items unlike real practice. Author names not recorded.
agent_relevance: Direct test that models cling to a familiar frame against counterevidence. Test S6 on items where the familiar answer is wrong.

source: Fugelsang, Stein, Green, Dunbar (2004) Theory and data interactions of the scientific mind, Can J Exp Psychol
finding: Search summary only: scientists in lab meetings were at first reluctant to treat inconsistent data as real, but repeated observations reduced this bias. The student companion study showed the same shift.
numbers: Secondhand: more than 50% of experiments in the labs Dunbar observed gave unexpected results. No sample sizes read.
limits: Not opened (PDF returned 404). Numbers are secondhand and unverified.
agent_relevance: Supports a repeat-then-accept rule: one anomaly is discounted, a replicated one is believed.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) The role of anomalous data in knowledge acquisition, Rev Educ Res 63(1)
finding: Search summaries say seven responses to anomalous data exist: ignore, reject, exclude, hold in abeyance, reinterpret, peripheral theory change, accept and change theory. Only the last changes the main theory.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened (403). The seven-category claim comes from an abstract and a critique.
agent_relevance: Name which of the seven the agent is doing. 'Reject' and 'reinterpret' are cheap defaults to guard against.

source: Student sensemaking with anomalous data (2024) CBE Life Sci Educ
finding: Students identify the anomaly, explain its cause, then choose to keep, remove, recollect or mitigate. The cause they attribute predicts the action.
numbers: N=6 students, up to four 1-hour think-aloud interviews. Coded resource counts: consider experimental context 19, select data to avoid anomalies 17, relative impact of anomaly 12, cross-reference data sources 11. Kappa 0.77. No percentages.
limits: Tiny sample; technical anomalies only; interviewer helped; Kuhn not cited.
agent_relevance: Cause attribution decides the action. Make the agent state a cause (tool error vs frame error) before it keeps, drops or switches.

source: Limon (2001) cognitive conflict as an instructional strategy (via Cambridge PSA abstract and search snippet)
finding: The PSA 1994 paper plans a naturalist account of anomaly in theory change; full text was paywalled. A separate critique reportedly finds that anomaly-induced conflict often fails to change theory.
numbers: None.
limits: Only an abstract extract was seen. The Limon claim comes from a search snippet and is unverified.
agent_relevance: Surprise alone does not cause a switch; supply the rival frame with the anomaly.

source: Kuhn (1962) The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
finding: From memory: normal science works inside a paradigm, anomalies are first absorbed, a crisis comes when they pile up and resist, and a rival paradigm replaces the old one. No count of anomalies is given.
numbers: No numbers. Not opened.
limits: Kuhn gives no threshold, so 'several independent failures' is our choice. Critics (Popper, Lakatos, Laudan) hold that anomalies alone never force replacement without a better rival (from memory).
agent_relevance: Do not claim Kuhn supports a fixed count. Switch only when failures are independent, located by code and a rival frame exists.

source: Bruner & Postman (1949) On the perception of incongruity: a paradigm
finding: From memory: with short exposure, people saw trick playing cards (a red spade) as normal; with longer exposure they hesitated, then saw the oddity. Kuhn used it as a model.
numbers: Not read; participant count is recalled and unverified.
limits: Old, small, perceptual not theoretical. I did not find a large modern replication.
agent_relevance: Check first that the agent notices an anomaly in its input at all, then test the switch.

source: Evidence gap note: Kuhn-style crisis trigger in LLM agents
finding: No study found this session that tests a 'switch frame after n independent failures' trigger with a measured threshold. Closest are Reflexion, the underthinking paper and the self-correction critiques.
numbers: WebSearch budget ran out before the Kuhn-LLM query; only fetches of arXiv, PMC and web pages were done.
limits: Absence in a narrow search is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: S6 count threshold is a design placeholder [D]. Run a dose test: switch after 1, 2, 3, 5 verified failures with a dwell-time floor, plus a resampling control.
